articles.title: Get The Entire Destiny 2 Experience At 75% Off For A Short Time
articles.description: Bungie may have stopped development on Destiny 2 , but that doesn’t mean that it’s over. Like the first game, its servers are still live and fairly active, and with Destiny 2’s excellent expansions, there are hundreds of hours of content waiting for both New Lights and returning Guardians to enjoy. As someone who has bought every expansion at release, seeing the entire Destiny 2 collection at 75% off is a remarkable deal, and one that I wholly recommend. I’ve got over 2,000 hours across both Destiny games, making them my second- and third-most-played games behind Minecraft. Even 12 years later, I still look back on the original fondly, and I’ve been a day-one player of both entries. It’s hard to put into words what makes Destiny so special, but I’ve got plenty of explanations for why Destiny 2 is one of the best FPS games ever–and why this deal shouldn’t be overlooked. You play as a Guardian (basically a superpower "Light"-wielding, gunslinging space wizard/warrior/assassin, depending on the class you pick). After being revived by the ever-present Traveler, you need to kill a bunch of bad guys. However, while you slay hordes of Hive, deal with the villainous Vex, or, well, the rest of the solar system’s enemies, you’ll uncover universe-spanning mysteries. The lore is deep, but you don’t have to go deep into it to have a good time; it’s definitely exciting if you decide to. While Destiny 2 itself is free-to-play (so you can go try it and see if you like it first), the expansions add a ridiculous amount of content, and personally, I wouldn’t play it without them anymore. Beyond Light adds the Darkness, the counterpart to the Light that powers Guardians, as the energy source for a new character subclass, while the excellent The Witch Queen sees you deal with Savathûn, one of the Hive gods, voiced by the brilliant Debra Wilson. Lightfall adds the Strand subclass, which is pretty much the best part of the DLC, admittedly, but it all leads into The Final Shape, which, safe to say, is Destiny’s peak. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sHqfh1EMF2k I won’t spoil the Light and Darkness Saga’s final DLC, the culmination of a decade of Destiny storytelling. What I will say is that it represents every reason I love Bungie’s world. The missions are amazing, the locations are beautiful, and the narrative proves exactly why the two games have captured millions of players. Our The Final Shape review gave it a 9/10, with Phil Hornshaw saying, “The Final Shape takes everything that’s good about Destiny [...] and brings them all together in ways the game has generally struggled to in the past.” I’ve bought every DLC at full price and never regretted it. However, when you have potentially thousands of hours of content at such a discounted price, it’s well worth giving it a chance. Right now, Destiny 2: The Collection (which includes everything in the game besides that pesky vaulted content) is just $19.24 / £15.94 at Fanatical . If you pour even half as much time as I did–say, 500 hours–that works out to about three cents per hour. Hard to not call that a bargain. Also, do yourself a favor and be a Warlock. I’ve spent the last decade maining the wizarding Guardian class, and I’m thankful I started back in the first Destiny with it. If you’re already a Warlock main, good on ya. Disclosure: GameSpot and Fanatical are both owned by Fandom. This story was created in collaboration with Fanatical's deals team.

articles.title: 'Terrified' Trump's 'freak out' at NBC host revealed a telling admission: conservative
articles.description: President Donald Trump raged at NBC News journalist Kristen Welker over the weekend after she questioned the worth of his electoral endorsements, and a conservative commentator said his threats betrayed a deeper anxiety. The "Meet the Press" host reported on the "mixed results" in his recent endorsements in GOP primary races, and the 80-year-old president accused her of “purposeful inaccuracy” and threatened that she would “be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment," which conservative Jonah Goldberg described as a telling admission. "I do think everyone's missing the actual political angle on this, though," Goldberg told "CNN This Morning," "which is, I agree with you the analogy, the Selzer poll is a good one, but specifically on this thing where Trump called [Bill] Maher or when he's freaking out at Kristen Welker, Trump is terrified that he's losing control of the Republican Party, and the idea ... of his unilateral imperial control over it, that it's the Trump party, and if the idea that his endorsements in primaries don't matter as much as they used to, that is the only thing that keeps a lot of Republicans in line is terror of him endorsing a primary opponent." "If it gets out that, oh my gosh, he's a lame duck and his endorsements inside his own coalition don't matter as they once did," Goldberg added. "That's why he's freaking out." Goldberg also argued the episode undermined the purpose of the Federal Communications Commission. "I think it's time for the FCC either to be dismantled or at least seriously re-evaluated how it does its job," Goldberg said. "It was built for an era of radio; it was updated for TV. It doesn't cover stuff on the internet already, and you know, with people under 30, they're basically getting everything through the internet already. So, like, figure out what the mission should be and maybe don't make and maybe redesign it. So a president can't do any of this stuff because it's gross." - YouTube youtu.be

articles.title: The Black Garden review – haunting study of growing up in war-torn Nagorno-Karabakh
articles.description: Alexis Pazoumian’s documentary follows Samvel and Avo, two preteen boys whose lives will be unavoidably scarred by brutal conflict After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, a decades-long territorial dispute exploded in the region of Nagorno-Karabakh, as its largely Armenian population fought against countless military campaigns from the Azerbaijani army. Shot over the course of three eventful years, which culminated in the surrender of Nagorno-Karabakh’s separatist government in 2023 , Alexis Pazoumian’s haunting documentary harnesses the collective turmoil that dominated generations of Armenians. From the elderly to the very young, the community are united by an unwavering sense of pride, one that carries them through never-ending bloodshed and displacement. The film opens with the harrowing sight of a bombed-out school in the small village of Talish, where childlike innocence contrasts with wartime trauma. Samvel and Avo, two preteen boys, roam through the wreckage and scavenge for remains of past normalcy, like the scattered notebooks left behind by their former classmates. The threat of the enemy, however, is drilled into every aspect of their daily life. At school, they learn how to assemble guns, and at family gatherings, they join in songs that speak of heroic valour. That the children here – boys and girls – will grow up to become soldiers is a foregone conclusion. Continue reading...

articles.title: Performance and belonging: Rio de Janeiro’s ballroom scene – photo essay
articles.description: A look at the ballroom scene across Maré, Lapa, Gamboa and the city centre. The photographer Juliana Bizzo has documented a movement born from Black and Latinx LGBTQ+ communities in the US that has more recently evolved in Rio, growing from the city’s first ball in 2016 My first encounter with Rio de Janeiro’s ballroom scene was in 2023, during Noite das Estrelas, an artistic occupation that moved through the streets of Maré. From the top of a sound truck, the performer and drag queen Preta Queen B Rull, of the Kiki House of Mamba Negra, sang as people followed her through the neighbourhood. Before we had even reached our destination, the procession had changed the rhythm of the street. Preta Queen B Rull performs from a sound truck during Noite das Estrelas. Continue reading...
